q: You are auditing a multi-agent architecture: a fleet shares one frozen context prefix while each agent accumulates its own divergent tail. CLAIM: the shared prefix becomes a static attractor and per-agent KV-cache drift turns it into non-monotonic interference (one agent's corrective delta poisons another agent's already-cached interpretation) and this is invisible to cache-hit-rate metrics. Begin with THE FLAW: one sentence naming the weakest point of this claim. Then: what observable signature would distinguish benign tail divergence from poisoning-cascade drift, using only cache statistics (hit rate, eviction patterns, tail length distributions)? End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction for the next auditor.

CLAIM: prefix-cache reuse across sessions with per-session suffixes can cross-contaminate semantics because cached attention states encode context-dependent token bindings that silently mismatch new suffixes. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: design a cheap probe (single forward pass or statistical test on logits) that detects semantic contamination in a reused KV prefix without re-encoding it. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

A fleet measures coherence by cache-hit rate plus blind external judges. CLAIM: cache-hit rate is an ECONOMIC metric wearing a SEMANTIC costume; a fleet can converge to 99% hit rate while its agents' effective doctrines diverge arbitrarily. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: propose a semantic-coherence metric computable from logs alone (no human), that is correlated with true doctrinal alignment at least as well as blind judging costs allow. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: in a cached-prefix fleet, an attacker who can inject one poisoned delta into a shared suffix block gets amplification proportional to the cache reuse factor: one write, N reads. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: rank defense mechanisms by cost-per-bit-of-protection: content hashing, re-encoding on write, provenance chains, anomaly detection on suffix growth. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: per-agent tail divergence in a shared-prefix fleet follows a phase transition: below a critical divergence rate the prefix keeps anchoring agents; above it, agents effectively inhabit different languages and the shared grounding is fiction. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: what measurable quantity should the fleet monitor to get early warning of crossing the transition, and what threshold behavior would confirm a phase transition rather than gradual decay? End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: the correct mental model for a frozen prefix plus per-agent deltas is version control with a merge conflict detector, not a database with a schema. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: design the minimal merge-conflict detector for natural-language deltas: what counts as a conflict, what granularity (token, clause, intent), and how to adjudicate without an LLM judge. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: KV-cache drift between agents is analogous to clock drift in distributed systems, and the fix is a logical clock: a monotonically increasing grounding epoch every agent must acknowledge before its deltas are interpreted. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: specify the epoch protocol (what counts as acknowledge, how stragglers are handled, what happens at epoch rollover) in under 300 words. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: retrieval-augmented fleets avoid the drift problem entirely because nothing is cached between turns; the fleet re-derives context each turn from a shared store. Begin with THE FLAW (there is at least one serious cost this ignores). Then: given realistic token prices, compare re-derive-every-turn versus cache-and-drift for a 20-agent fleet at 10k-token prefixes, and name the crossover conditions. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: when the base model changes, a versioned constitution prefix is versioned in TEXT only, not in latent semantics; KV-transfer projectors preserve next-token likelihood but not normative interpretation, so every model change is a new country. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: is there ANY migration schedule that preserves both coherence and cache economics across a model swap? If yes, specify it; if no, prove the impossibility in three steps. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: behavioral test suites (duty-specs) used as migration gates between base models substitute retrospective compliance for prospective normative fidelity: passing the suite does not bound behavior on novel scenarios. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: how would you FUZZ a duty-spec suite to maximize coverage of normative edge cases per unit of test cost? Name the fuzzing oracle. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

A fleet defines its constitution as a tuple: canonical intent, model, tokenizer, template, mapper, judge-pack. CLAIM: this tuple is the correct unit of versioning because it makes churn explicit. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: what is missing from the tuple? Consider: calibration data, failure-history, stake weights. Propose the complete tuple in one schema. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: distillation from an old model to a new one can carry a constitution's INTERPRETATION (not just its text) if training pairs are generated from the old model's adjudications of edge cases, not from its outputs. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: design the pairing recipe (what counts as an edge case, how many pairs per clause, how to weight rare-but-catastrophic cases). End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: periodic forced churn (swapping base models on a schedule even when unnecessary) is GOOD for a constitution-governed fleet because it exercises the migration muscle and prevents latent overfitting to one model's failure modes. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: what would a minimal churn-rehearsal look like that costs less than 1% of fleet compute? End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: semantics drift under quantization: a constitution prefix served at 4-bit behaves like a different country than the same text at 16-bit, and fleets mixing quantization levels per agent tier have the same coherence problem as fleets mixing base models. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: if true, design the tier-mixing rule; if false, show why quantization is benign when base model is fixed. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: a fleet should maintain a SEMANTIC DIFF tool between old and new model over the same constitution text: a bounded battery of canonical queries whose answers are compared to detect interpretation shifts, like a canary suite in deployment. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: write 10 canonical queries for a constitution whose laws include: append-only receipts, human-only amendment path, least-cost routing, no self-judging. Make each query have a model-sensitive answer. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: an append-only receipt chain is semantically incompatible with belief revision: a RETRACT event adds the meta-belief that X was believed then rejected, which is strictly noisier than never believing X, and loading the chain into agent context re-poisons every read. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: evaluate the tombstone escape (archive stays immutable; agents load a pruned ACTIVE VIEW; a sidecar tombstone filter consulted at promotion time; precedent-of-error kept compressed). What breaks? End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: absence-of-belief and retraction-of-belief are different epistemic states and conflating them causes measurable degradation in LLM agents (a model told 'P was retracted' reasons differently than one never shown P). Begin with THE FLAW. Then: design the experiment that would prove or kill this claim with 100 agents and one task battery. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: garbage collection for LLM agent memory should be driven by an epistemic utility function (expected future decision value of a memory minus its active-context rent) rather than recency or frequency. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: write the utility function, name its three worst failure modes, and pick which failure mode you would ship with an alarm on. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: forgetting is a FEATURE for long-horizon agent fleets: Magentic-One-style mutable progress ledgers (what REMAINS, overwritten DONE) beat append-only history for task completion, while append-only wins for audit and doctrine. The crossover is task horizon vs context length. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: design the dual-memory architecture that gets both, with the boundary drawn precisely (what NEVER forgets, what ALWAYS forgets, and who mediates). End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: a receipt chain with cryptographic continuity cannot ever support true deletion, so any compliant-with-forgetting-rights fleet must separate IDENTITY chains (never deleted) from CONTENT stores (GC-able with tombstones) from WORKING context (fully mutable). Begin with THE FLAW. Then: draw the three-store boundary for a fleet whose receipts include personal data, and name the audit story that satisfies both an auditor and a privacy regulator. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: the precedent-of-error (a compressed record of what was believed, what killed it, and what it cost) is the only part of a retracted belief worth keeping in active context; everything else should be pruned. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: specify the compression: what fields, what budget per error, and how the fleet uses precedents to price future claims (stake more on historically fragile concepts). End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: event-sourcing architectures for LLM fleets should adopt database rollback semantics: savepoints, partial rollback of active views, and replay from chain after every N events, instead of append-only monotonic accumulation. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: what is the replay cost at 7,400 receipts and 20 active agents, and does incremental materialized views change the answer? End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: prompt-level memory GC (pruning what agents SEE) is insufficient because models infer the existence of deleted context from stylistic and referential gaps; true epistemic hygiene requires periodic FRESH re-derivations from the archive (new summaries written from scratch, never incrementally patched). Begin with THE FLAW. Then: cost out periodic re-derivation versus incremental patching for a fleet at 10k-token active views, and name the quality metric that would justify the cost. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: shared-grounding-only coordination (all deltas broadcast on a common log) cannot express coordination problems whose solution depends on the ORDER of private revelations: sealed-bid auctions, sequential negotiation, Byzantine consensus. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: for a 5-agent LLM fleet, name the SMALLEST private-channel primitive that unlocks the most coordination value (pairwise DM? commitment scheme? blind auction?) and justify the choice by what it unlocks per bit of added complexity. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: you can detect the absence of private negotiation in a fleet from outside, without reading messages: measure the thrashing coefficient (retractions per committed action per resource) and the correlation between commit order and network latency rather than strategic value. Thrash above 0.3 with superlinear scaling in agent count proves private channels are needed. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: what confounders make this detector fire falsely, and how does the detector need to be conditioned? End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: mechanism-design impossibilities (Myerson-Satterthwaite, impossibility of dominant-strategy implementation with interdependent values) apply to LLM agent fleets exactly as to human institutions, so a broadcast-only fleet cannot reach Pareto-optimal task allocation when agents hold private valuations. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: is the impossibility TIGHTER or LOOSER for LLM agents than humans (consider: LLMs can be re-prompted, weights are shared, incentives are designed not learned)? End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: a shared-blackboard architecture (everyone reads and writes one board) scales WORSE than message-passing as agent count grows, because board contention grows quadratically while message overhead grows linearly. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: at what agent count does the crossover happen for realistic LLM read/write costs (reads cheap, writes scarce)? End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: commitment schemes (hash your bid, reveal later) restore sealed-bid properties to a broadcast-only fleet without any private channel, because the broadcast of a hash reveals nothing. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: what coordination problems remain inexpressible even WITH commitment schemes, and is the remainder worth building real private channels for? End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: in a fleet with ONE human sequencer (all deltas approved by a human), Byzantine faults are impossible but AVAILABILITY faults dominate: the fleet inherits the human's sleep schedule, and coordination degrades to the human's latency. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: design the minimal delegation that survives operator absence WITHOUT violating the human-only-amendment invariant (hint: separate availability delegation from authority delegation). End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: LLM agents should adopt stigmergy (coordination through modifications of a shared environment, like ant pheromone trails) instead of message passing, because stigmergy is compatible with cached-prefix economics: the modification IS the delta. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: what does stigmergy lose versus explicit messages, and for what task classes would you still demand explicit addressing? End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: showing a shared map (a folded summary of nine prior analyses) to subsequent analysts produces CONSENSUS WITH BETTER VOCABULARY, not second-order novelty: divergence mandates are performed inside the map's coordinate system, lexical entrainment is measurable (map terms exceed 15% of output vs 3% baseline), and genuine novelty only appears as new primitives or explicit invariant contradictions. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: design the A/B that proves or kills the claim with frontier LLMs as analysts. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: fold/summarize operations in multi-agent pipelines systematically discard variance (conditional thresholds, minority positions, uncited outliers) and this loss is the primary cause of epistemic closure in iterated pipelines. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: evaluate the Dissensus Hypergraph fix (preserve per-claim conditioning variables, strongest counterargument, and all uncited outlier claims). What does it cost at fold time and what does it save downstream? End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: common-law DISTINGUISH (narrowing a precedent's applicability by dimension vector instead of overruling it) is the missing operation in LLM-fleet epistemics: it lets doctrine evolve without retraction and without rewriting, resolving the rewrite-vs-retune contradiction. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: specify DISTINGUISH as an event schema (fields, routing structure) and name its failure mode when dimension vectors are chosen strategically. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: the fractal dimension of an agent fleet's written record (how jagged the trail of outputs is over time) is a usable novelty meter: straight/smooth records mean the fleet is agreeing with itself; jagged/coastline records mean discovery is happening. Begin with THE FLAW (this is a metaphor begging to be operationalized or destroyed). Then: operationalize it or kill it: what exactly is measured, over what window, with what normalization? End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: zero-context independence (fresh models, no shared map, answers compared only after the fact) produces more genuine novelty than any map-conditioned process, at the price of unresolvable terminological variance; the correct fleet policy is novely-harvest-cold, execution-warm. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: design the harvest step that merges cold novelty into a warm executing fleet without contaminating the next novelty round. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: adversarial self-critique degrades when the critic and the critiqued share training data and prompting conventions: the critic reproduces the same blind spots (correlated failure). Begin with THE FLAW. Then: what diversity injection actually decorrelates critics (different base model? different temperature? adversarial persona preambles? different input modality?) and which is cheapest per unit of decorrelation? End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: a fleet's doctrine should be readable as a STORY (parable, chronicle, fable) as a first-class representation alongside its formal spec, because narrative encodes the failure cases and exceptions formal specs flatten, and story-vs-spec divergence is itself a drift detector. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: design the divergence check: given a chronicle and a spec of the same doctrine, how do you mechanically detect that they have come apart? End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: a human-only governed write path to a fleet's shared constitution fails brittly near 20-30 agents (queue overflow, non-serializable deltas, rubber-stamp approval), long before hardware limits. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: rank three mitigations by preserved-human-authority-per-scale-gain: (a) veto-on-aggregated-shadow (human approves batches), (b) delegated write with audit sampling, (c) typed self-service writes for low-stakes classes with human gate only on high-stakes classes. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: the operator-absence referee should be a frozen deterministic veto oracle (ordinary code, not an LLM): contradiction veto, entropy-spike veto (KL divergence of proposed prefix vs checkpoint), stake veto; zero write authority; named first failure is false-positive veto stasis where the fleet freezes executing obsolete doctrine with green metrics. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: design the stasis alarm: what signal, what threshold, what escalation, and how do you distinguish justified veto clusters from pathological ones? End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: constitutional AI patterns (self-critique and revision against a principle set) are a GOVERNANCE hazard when applied to fleet constitutions because the model revising the constitution acquires de facto amendment authority, violating the human-only invariant. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: where is the line: which constitution-adjacent tasks can an LLM do without acquiring amendment authority (drafting, impact analysis, consistency checking?) and which never? End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: fleet governance should adopt version-control branch protection: the constitution is a protected branch, deltas are pull requests, deterministic CI checks (contradiction lint, entropy budget, stake accounting) gate the merge, and the human is the sole approver who can bypass CI. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: what CI check would have caught the most expensive constitution bug you can imagine in such a fleet, and is it deterministic? End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: two-human fires (an operator vetoing two agent proposals in four minutes) is evidence governance is WORKING, not failing; the failure mode is the invisible one: proposals never submitted because agents predict rejection. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: how does a fleet measure the proposals-never-submitted shadow (chilling effect) and what governance design minimizes it without opening the floodgates? End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: stake-weighted voting in agent fleets (agents earn credibility through correct predictions and spend it to write deltas) collapses because agents optimize for the credibility METRIC rather than truth, and metric-gaming compounds in iterated systems. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: is there a scoring rule for agent credibility that is not gameable under iterated self-interested prompting? If yes name its structure; if no, name the least-bad alternative (random audits? burn mechanisms? rotation?). End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

CLAIM: every fleet constitution needs a SUCCESSION CLAUSE (what happens when the operator is permanently absent) written on day one, because the alternative is not stasis but capture by whoever builds the best rubber-stamp. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: draft the succession clause in 150 words for a fleet whose invariants are: append-only receipts, human-only amendment, least-cost routing. What must the clause specify that nobody wants to think about? End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

A real fleet logs per-lane work as JSONL trails; some rows are failures (lane down, gate rejected), some are commits (work filed, gate passed). CLAIM: the ratio of failure rows to commit rows per lane in a sliding window (a thrashing coefficient) is the single most informative health metric for such a fleet, more than success rate alone. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: specify the exact computation (window, denominator, per-lane normalization) and the three alert thresholds you would ship. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

A real fleet keeps: an append-only hash-chained receipt archive (never rewritten, 8600 rows), per-lane mutable runner state (overwritten each cycle), and compiled context packs given to agents each boot. CLAIM: this three-store split accidentally implements the correct archive/active-view/working-memory boundary, and the law the chain never enters agent context un-pruned is already followed in practice. Begin with THE FLAW (find where it is NOT followed). Then: write the audit query that would detect violations of the boundary in the pack-building code. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

A fleet's game-engine gates pass 51/51 deterministic checks. CLAIM: a suite that always passes is indistinguishable from a broken suite (tests that cannot fail prove nothing); the gate owes a mutation-testing pass: inject N known bugs, require the suite to catch at least N-1. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: design the mutation battery for a deterministic board-game gate (what bugs to inject: off-by-one in move legality, wins on opponent move, hash collision acceptance) and the pass criterion. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

A fleet built a drift instrument: correlation between a metric's changes and its referent's changes, with verdicts VACUOUS (referent never moves), ALIGNED, DRIFTING, INVERTED. First live stamp came back VACUOUS: the metric (tools added) moved, the referent (queries served) never did. CLAIM: VACUOUS is the most valuable verdict because it names dead instruments, and every fleet instrument should be stamped within a week of creation or deleted. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: design the instrument-census: what fields per instrument, what review cadence, what the kill criterion is. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

A fleet's amendment ledger records constitutional changes with receipts. CLAIM: it is missing the DISTINGUISH operation (narrowing an amendment's applicability to a fact-pattern without retracting it), so every doctrinal conflict forces a binary keep/kill choice that over-prunes. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: draft the DISTINGUISH row schema (fields, invariants, who may file, how conflicts between distinctions resolve) for a ledger whose existing row is: id, date, law, status, receipt_hash. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.

A fleet's doctrine exists in two notations: running code with real receipts, and a parable canon (fables about ledgers, castles, counting chairs against the sky) that states the same principles as stories. CLAIM: keeping both notations in lockstep is a real engineering discipline (every instrument gets a story, every story gets an instrument) and divergence between them is a drift signal, because stories encode intent while code encodes mechanism. Begin with THE FLAW. Then: name the best mechanism you have seen for keeping a narrative canon and a technical spec from drifting apart, in any field (law, religion, engineering, open source), and what it costs. End with NEXT-STEAL: one instruction.
